assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks at the 1e-18 level are a measurement advance of the kind I value most: the magic-wavelength idea turned thousands of atoms into a quantum-limited oscillator and opened redefinition of the second, relativistic geodesy, tests of fundamental constants and dark-matter searches. The clarity of the metric (fractional uncertainty, stability, frequency ratios) and the field-opening impact are exceptional.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength optical lattice concept; Ye led the demonstration of systematic uncertainty and stability at 1e-18 and the many-body (Sr lattice, spin-exchange) clock. Two laureates give a clean configuration; other clock groups (ion clocks, NIST, PTB, Hall and Hansch already recognised for the comb) are not credited here, and I would note that ion-clock work was recognised earlier.
assessment.maturity: Multiple independent labs (JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, NIST, SYRTE) reproduce comparable performance and clock comparisons across continents. The interpretation is stable and the timing is good, with redefinition of the SI second under discussion.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2005 and 2012 recognition of frequency combs and ion-control for clocks, which could be argued to have covered part of the territory.

Whether Katori's prediction and Ye's realisation are weighted equally, and whether other contributors (e.g. Takamoto, Lemonde, Hollberg, Ludlow) deserve mention, is not resolved by the supplied credit.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit QED created a controllable, strongly coupled light-matter platform with coherence times improved by orders of magnitude, enabling transmon qubits, dispersive readout, quantum-limited amplification and the leading solid-state quantum processors. The work is original, experimentally concrete and has opened a very large field.
assessment.attribution: The 2004 theory (Blais, Huang, Wallraff, Girvin, Schoelkopf) and the Yale/ETH experiments (Wallraff, Schoelkopf) are the decisive contributions; the transmon came from the Yale group. Four names are credited, so one needs to be dropped; I would pick the experimental pair plus Girvin, though Blais is an equally defensible theory co-author.
assessment.maturity: Highly mature and independently confirmed by many groups and industrial programmes. Timing is delicate because the 2025 prize recognised macroscopic quantum tunnelling in superconducting circuits, which sits close to this topic.
uncertainties: Proximity to the 2025 Nobel Prize in Physics could make recognition so soon seem repetitive.
Boundary between Girvin and Blais, and the contribution of the transmon inventors (Koch et al.) to the credit, is not settled.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Matter-wave interferometry with atoms became a precision-measurement tool for gravity, gravity gradients, rotation and tests of the equivalence principle and the fine-structure constant, with real devices (gravimeters, gyroscopes) and a clear route to field applications. This is the kind of new measurement method that opens nature to observation.
assessment.attribution: Bordé (atom interferometer theory and the Ramsey-Bordé interferometer), Pritchard (first atom interferometers, nanofabricated gratings) and Kasevich (Raman-pulse atom-interferometer inertial sensing, large-momentum-transfer) are all decisive. Chu's related work was recognised in 1997. Schmiedmayer is also credited and would be a close fourth.
assessment.maturity: Well confirmed across several groups with commercial gravimeters; the long-baseline and space tests remain in progress, so the strongest fundamental-physics payoffs are still developing.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 1997 prize (laser cooling) and the 2001 BEC prize could be raised.
Whether the prize should centre on interferometer principle (Bordé, Pritchard) or on sensing performance (Kasevich) is a genuine allocation question.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Cirac-Zoller proposal and subsequent experiments with trapped ions established the first fully controllable quantum gates, entanglement of many qubits, and quantum simulation, with high-fidelity operations that set the benchmark for quantum information hardware. Experimentally and conceptually foundational.
assessment.attribution: Cirac and Zoller supplied the 1995 proposal; Blatt built the leading experimental programme (entanglement of up to 14 ions, quantum-computing demonstrations). Wineland, honoured in 2012, did the early ion-control work, and Monroe and others also contributed to the demonstrations, which weakens a clean three-person allocation.
assessment.maturity: Very mature and widely reproduced; commercial platforms exist. Part of the territory has already been recognised via the 2012 prize, so the room for a new prize is narrower.
uncertainties: Overlap with Wineland's 2012 prize and the possibility that Monroe belongs in any prize configuration but is not credited here.
Cirac and Zoller also appear in other lattice and Rydberg candidates, which complicates the combined allocation.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical detection and coherent control of single NV centres gave a room-temperature solid-state qubit and a nanoscale sensor for magnetic field, temperature and strain, with applications from NMR on single molecules to biology. It is a measurement-driven advance that reaches beyond physics, which I find compelling.
assessment.attribution: Wrachtrup demonstrated single-NV optical detection (1997) and Jelezko the coherent control and nuclear-spin registers; Lukin led quantum-sensing and quantum-register developments. Gruber, Awschalom and others also contributed to the field; Wrachtrup is also credited in B033, so the prize design must avoid double counting.
assessment.maturity: Independently reproduced in many labs and increasingly commercial, though sensitivity records and practical advantages over alternative sensors are still being established.
uncertainties: Overlap with B033 (optical interfaces to spins in solids) that shares Wrachtrup and could be treated as part of the same discovery.
Whether the practical sensing impact is yet at the level of a prize-defining breakthrough.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The ATLAS and CMS detectors were extraordinary instruments that made the Higgs boson discovery possible, and detector and trigger technology is a measurement achievement in its own right. The scientific outcome is among the most important in particle physics.
assessment.attribution: Della Negra, Jenni and Virdee are the founding spokespersons and conceivers of the experiments. The Higgs mechanism was recognised in 2013, and a prize for the experiment builders is an unusual configuration with some risk of the thousands of collaboration members being under-credited.
assessment.maturity: The discovery was confirmed independently by two experiments and subsequently by couplings measurements, so confirmation is excellent. The recognition is timely if the committee wishes to honour the experimental side.
uncertainties: Whether the prize rules and the Committee's tradition support honouring experiment leadership rather than a discovery by individuals.
Credit for the two collaborations is spread over very many contributors, so any three-person set is contestable.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The quantum cascade laser is a genuine invention: a semiconductor laser based on intersubband transitions engineered by bandstructure, giving mid-infrared and terahertz sources that enable trace-gas spectroscopy, sensing and imaging. It is a clear instrument-level advance with broad real-world impact.
assessment.attribution: Capasso, Faist and Cho were the Bell Labs team that made the 1994 demonstration, with Faist the first author and Capasso the leader; Cho supplied molecular-beam-epitaxy growth. Kazarinov and Suris proposed intersubband gain in 1971, which raises a historical priority question that is not in the credited names.
assessment.maturity: Mature, with commercial devices and wide adoption for over two decades. Timing is fine, and recognition is arguably overdue relative to impact.
uncertainties: Priority issue of the Kazarinov-Suris 1971 proposal relative to the Bell Labs realisation.
Whether the Committee considers this physics or primarily device engineering.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ultracold atoms in optical lattices realised Hubbard-type models, with the superfluid-to-Mott transition and later quantum-gas microscopes giving site-resolved observation of many-body states. The ability to measure strongly correlated systems at single-site level is a notable experimental advance.
assessment.attribution: Greiner (Mott insulator and microscopy), Bloch (superfluid-Mott transition, microscopy and simulation) and Esslinger (fermionic Hubbard systems) are the decisive experimentalists; Cirac and Zoller (also in B018) supplied the Jaksch-Zoller theory, so a theory-experiment split is possible. Five names are credited and only three can be selected.
assessment.maturity: Well reproduced across many groups, though the quantum-simulation claims for open problems such as the Hubbard model phase diagram are still being settled, so the practical payoff is partly in the future.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2001 BEC prize and with other candidates sharing Cirac and Zoller.
Whether quantum simulation has yet produced decisive new physics beyond demonstration of known models.
